reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / ACR-EULAR classification criteria
clinicalPearls: A pauci-immune, non-granulomatous necrotising small-vessel vasculitis, most strongly associated with perinuclear ANCA directed against myeloperoxidase
The classic presentation is a pulmonary-renal syndrome with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and, in severe cases, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Unlike granulomatosis with polyangiitis, it lacks destructive upper-airway granulomas, and unlike EGPA it lacks asthma and eosinophilia
Palpable purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, and constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and fever are common accompaniments
Renal biopsy typically shows focal necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis with scant immune deposits (pauci-immune)
Remission induction uses glucocorticoids combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, with plasma exchange reserved for selected severe presentations
Relapse risk is lower than in PR3-associated disease but chronic kidney injury frequently persists
reference.pathophysiology: Microscopic polyangiitis is a systemic pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitis within the ANCA-associated spectrum. Circulating anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies prime and activate neutrophils, which adhere to and degranulate against endothelium, releasing reactive oxygen species and proteolytic enzymes that produce necrotising inflammation of capillaries, venules, and arterioles. In the kidney this yields a focal segmental necrotising and crescentic glomerulonephritis with minimal immunoglobulin deposition, and in the lung it can cause alveolar capillaritis with haemorrhage. Unlike granulomatosis with polyangiitis, granuloma formation is characteristically absent.
additionalInvestigations: ANCA testing with anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase-3 specificities
Urinalysis and microscopy for dysmorphic haematuria and red cell casts
Renal function and urine protein quantification
Chest imaging and, where indicated, bronchoscopy for alveolar haemorrhage
Renal or other tissue biopsy demonstrating pauci-immune necrotising vasculitis
Anti-GBM antibody testing to exclude overlapping disease
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine with active urinary sediment indicating crescentic glomerulonephritis
Haemoptysis and hypoxaemia suggesting diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Progressive sensorimotor deficits from mononeuritis multiplex
Oliguria or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury
reference.prognosis: Prompt immunosuppression induces remission in most patients, but many are left with chronic kidney disease and some progress to end-stage renal failure. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and advanced renal impairment at presentation predict worse outcomes.
pitfalls: Delaying biopsy and treatment while awaiting ANCA serology in a deteriorating patient
Failing to distinguish MPA from anti-GBM disease, which alters urgency and use of plasma exchange
Overlooking alveolar haemorrhage when haemoptysis is minimal but haemoglobin falls
Attributing pauci-immune crescentic nephritis to another cause without checking ANCA
references: ACR-EULAR classification criteria for microscopic polyangiitis
management: Induce remission with high-dose glucocorticoids combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Add the C5a-receptor antagonist avacopan to reduce cumulative glucocorticoid exposure
Reserve plasma exchange for severe presentations such as diffuse alveolar haemorrhage or severe, advancing renal failure
Maintain remission with rituximab or azathioprine to prevent relapse
Support failing organs with renal replacement therapy for severe kidney injury and respiratory support for alveolar haemorrhage
Give prophylaxis against Pneumocystis, bone protection and vaccination while immunosuppressed
Monitor renal function, urinalysis, ANCA titre and drug toxicity to detect relapse and complications
Manage jointly with rheumatology, nephrology and respiratory teams
